claim_1.claim: Bulk RNA-seq assay analysis of platelet-rich plasma from 28 young adults, 20 community-dwelling older adults, and 17 skilled nursing facility-resident older adults before influenza vaccination (day 0) showed higher platelet activation pathways, Rho GTPase effector pathways, mitochondrial genes, and PF4 and PPBP expression in older groups versus young adults, with translation-related RNAs decreased from Young to Older (Comm) to Older (SNF).

sources.quote: Platelet activation pathways were significantly enriched in Older (Comm) compared with young adults, as were Rho GTPase effector pathways mediating the activation response (Aslan & McCarty, 2013 ) and mitochondrial genes (Table 2 , Extended Data Figure S2b ). Notably, activation pathways in platelets from Older (SNF) adults were also significantly increased compared to Older (Comm) adults.

Indeed, there was a strong correlation of the first principal component (PC1) (which accounted for over 72% of the variance (Figure 1a )) with both age ( r = 0.63, p = 2.12e−08) and platelet activation (as represented by Platelet Factor‐4 ( PF4 ) and Pro‐platelet Basic Protein ( PPBP , Figure 1b ). Notably, PF4 and PPBP were correlated with age ( r = 0.57, 0.49; p = 7.2e−07, 3.2e−05, respectively) and frailty ( r = 0.54, 0.52; p = 3.3e−06; 6.15e−6, respectively).
In contrast to the age‐associated increase in platelet activation RNAs, RNAs in pathways related to translation decreased with age and SNF resident status.

We isolated platelet‐rich plasma (PRP) from blood samples of participants obtained prior to vaccination (Day 0) and at Days 2, 7, and 28 post‐vaccine for isolation of RNA and elucidation of the platelet transcriptome via RNA‐seq.

We enrolled 28 young adults (age 21–35 years), 20 community‐dwelling older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (Comm)), and 17 older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (SNF)) who were residents of a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in greater New Haven, Connecticut (Table 1 ).

comparison.finding: Older (Comm) had higher platelet activation pathways, Rho GTPase effector pathways, mitochondrial genes, and PF4 and PPBP expression than young adults; translation-related RNAs were decreased relative to young adults.
Older (SNF) had higher platelet activation pathways, mitochondrial genes, and PF4 and PPBP expression than young adults; translation-related RNAs were decreased relative to young adults.
Older (SNF) had higher platelet activation pathways than Older (Comm), with translation-related RNAs decreased from Older (Comm) to Older (SNF).

claim_2.claim: Bulk RNA-seq assay analysis of platelet-rich plasma from participants sampled before influenza vaccination (day 0) and at days 2, 7, and 28 after vaccination (day 2, day 7, and day 28) showed distinct post-vaccination platelet activation RNA trajectories by group: Component 1 increased and remained stable in young adults, Component 2 showed a sustained decrease in Older (SNF), and Component 5 showed a drop then return toward baseline in Older (Comm); translation-related RNAs showed inverse trajectories.

sources.quote: Component 1 was associated with young adults, and represents a temporal expression pattern where RNA expression increased post‐vaccination and remained stable. In Component 2, which was associated with Older (SNF) adults, pre‐vaccination RNA levels experienced a sustained drop post‐vaccination and in Component 5, associated with Older (Comm) adults, pre‐vaccination RNA levels experienced a drop followed by a rise back to pre‐vaccination levels.
Pathways involving platelet degranulation, platelet activation, and hemostasis were significantly over‐represented (platelet activation genes PF4 and PPBP were members of this intersecting set).

We observed that expression of these RNAs tended to have higher pre‐vaccination levels which then decreased in young adults, while pre‐vaccination levels were lower and increased in Older (SNF) adults, with intermediate dynamics in Older (Comm) adults (Extended Data Figure S3 ).
Therefore, the negative correlation between platelet activation and translation gene RNA levels observed at pre‐vaccination was maintained following vaccination.
Blood samples were collected prior to vaccination (day 0) and follow‐up days 2, 7, and 28.

comparison.finding: In young adults, Component 1 platelet activation RNA expression increased post-vaccination and remained stable.
In young adults, Component 1 platelet activation RNA expression remained stable after its post-vaccination increase.
In young adults, Component 1 platelet activation RNA expression remained stable through day 28.
In Older (SNF), Component 2 platelet activation RNA levels showed a sustained decrease from pre-vaccination after vaccination.
In Older (SNF), Component 2 platelet activation RNA levels remained decreased at later post-vaccination time points.
In Older (SNF), Component 2 platelet activation RNA levels remained decreased through day 28.
In Older (Comm), Component 5 platelet activation RNA levels dropped after vaccination.
In Older (Comm), Component 5 platelet activation RNA levels rose after the initial drop.
In Older (Comm), Component 5 platelet activation RNA levels returned toward baseline by day 28.

At pre-vaccination, platelet activation and translation-related RNAs showed inverse trajectories between young adults and Older (SNF), and this negative correlation was maintained following vaccination.

At pre-vaccination, platelet activation and translation-related RNAs showed inverse trajectories between young adults and Older (Comm), and this negative correlation was maintained following vaccination.

Older (SNF) and Older (Comm) showed distinct platelet activation RNA trajectories post-vaccination: sustained decrease in Component 2 for Older (SNF) versus drop then return toward baseline in Component 5 for Older (Comm).

claim_3.claim: Bulk RNA-seq assay analysis of platelet-rich plasma from young adults showed that vaccine high responders versus low responders differed in platelet activation RNA trajectories after influenza vaccination (day 0), with Component 2 RNAs decreasing on days 7-28 in high responders but remaining stable in low responders, and more than 50% of top Component 2 RNAs including PF4 and PPBP differentially expressed at day 28.

sources.quote: Among young high responders ( n = 7), Component 2 RNAs decreased in expression on days 7–28, whereas in low responders ( n = 9) the expression levels remained stable (Figure 6a ).

we performed a DE analysis on the set of top 5% scoring RNAs from Component 2 between young adult high‐ and low responders at each day post‐vaccination, and found that more than 50% of the RNAs were significantly DE on day 28, while there were no significant differences at the other timepoints (Figure 6a ). These genes include PF4 and PPBP and are enriched in pathways associated with platelet response (Figure 6b,c ).
Blood samples were collected prior to vaccination (day 0) and follow‐up days 2, 7, and 28.

comparison.finding: At day 7, Component 2 platelet activation RNAs were decreased in high responders but remained stable in low responders.

At day 28, more than 50% of top Component 2 RNAs were significantly differentially expressed between high and low responders, including PF4 and PPBP; Component 2 RNAs decreased in high responders but remained stable in low responders.

claim_4.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of platelet-rich plasma from a subset of participants at baseline before influenza vaccination (day 0) and days 2 and 7 after vaccination (day 2 and day 7) showed significantly higher surface CD62p, CD40L, and CD63 expression in community-dwelling older adults versus young adults at all measured days, while skilled nursing facility-resident older adults had significantly lower expression than community-dwelling older adults and were generally comparable to young adults except for higher day 0 CD62p.

sources.quote: The levels of surface expression of all three proteins were significantly increased in platelets from Older (Comm), compared to young adults at day 0, 2, and 7, suggesting an age‐associated increase in platelet activation.

However, surface expression in Older (SNF) adults was significantly decreased compared to Older (Comm), with Older (SNF) activation marker surface expression comparable to that of platelets from young adults (with the exception of Day 0 CD62p expression in Older (SNF) adults, which was significantly higher compared to platelets from young adults) (Figure 5c,f ).
Platelet function was further assessed by flow cytometry at Days 0, 2, and 7 post‐vaccine in a subset of participants where flow cytometry was done immediately after PRP isolation.
The activation status of platelets was further estimated as percentage of CD41+ CD40L+, CD41+CD62P+ and CD41+CD63+ particles.

claim_5.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of platelet-rich plasma from Young (n = 14), Older (Comm) (n = 17), and Older (SNF) (n = 17) participants at days 2 and 7 after influenza vaccination (day 2 and day 7), normalized to baseline before vaccination (day 0), showed that CD62p protein changes paralleled SELP RNA changes, with the highest fold-change in young adults followed by Older (Comm) and then Older (SNF), whereas CD40L and CD63 protein did not parallel their RNA expression.

sources.quote: We found that expression of SELP RNA at day 2 and day 7 post‐vaccine, normalized to day 0, followed the pattern of platelet activation RNA levels identified by tensor decomposition analysis (Figure 4 ), with highest fold‐change in young adults, followed by Older (Comm) and Older (SNF) adults (Figure 5b ). Notably, the surface expression of CD62p/SELP protein at these post‐vaccine time points relative to day 0 closely resembled the RNA expression pattern (Figure 5d ). We did not observe a similar parallel relationship between normalized RNA expression and protein expression for CD40L and CD63 (Figure 5e,f ).
Blood samples were collected prior to vaccination (day 0) and follow‐up days 2, 7, and 28.

claim_6.claim: Hemagglutination Inhibition analysis of serum from 28 young adults, 20 community-dwelling older adults, and 17 skilled nursing facility-resident older adults collected before influenza vaccination (day 0) and at day 28 after vaccination (day 28) was used to derive maxRBA responder groups, and Bulk RNA-seq assay of platelet-rich plasma before vaccination (day 0) showed 12 RNAs upregulated and 7 downregulated in high versus low responders, including THRB, BLZF1, MPIG6B, and CCR1 among the upregulated RNAs.

sources.quote: Influenza vaccine antibody response was measured using a standard hemagglutination inhibition assay (HAI). To correct for the inverse correlation between pre‐vaccine HAI titer and fold‐increase post‐vaccine, we employed maximum residual after baseline adjustment (maxRBA), a metric which models HAI titer fold changes as an exponential function of strain‐specific baseline titers and selects the maximum residual across strains (Avey et al., 2020 ) (Figure S1 ). maxRBA was used to classify high and low vaccine responders for assessment of platelet transcriptomic differences in vaccine responsiveness.

we performed a DE analysis of high‐ vs. low responders in the pre‐vaccination state, and identified 12 upregulated and 7 down‐regulated RNAs in high responders; upregulated RNAs included THRB, BLZF1, MPIG6B, and CCR1 (Table S7 ).

We isolated platelet‐rich plasma (PRP) from blood samples of participants obtained prior to vaccination (Day 0) and at Days 2, 7, and 28 post‐vaccine for isolation of RNA and elucidation of the platelet transcriptome via RNA‐seq.

We enrolled 28 young adults (age 21–35 years), 20 community‐dwelling older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (Comm)), and 17 older adults (age ≥65 years) (Older (SNF)) who were residents of a skilled nursing facility (SNF) in greater New Haven, Connecticut (Table 1 ).
Antibody response to vaccination was assessed using serum samples obtained at day 0 and 28 using a standard hemagglutination inhibition assay (Frey et al., 2010 ).

comparison.finding: Bulk RNA-seq of platelet-rich plasma before vaccination at day 0 identified 12 RNAs upregulated and 7 downregulated in high versus low responders; upregulated RNAs included THRB, BLZF1, MPIG6B, and CCR1.
